In this lesson, you will learn about unijunction transistors (UJT's) used as oscillators.
INTRODUCTIONM
UJT oscillator circuits are simple, comprising of just a few components.
Even though few components are used, UJT oscillators produce three output signals.
A voltage switch, (UJT Transistor), is controlled by a circuit to produce an oscillator.

DISCUSSION
The purpose of the circuit is to act as an oscillator producing a sawtooth wave, changing DC power to AC power.
Vcc applies the bias voltage for Q1..............................
R1 and C1 form an RC circuit that applies emitter voltage to Q1...
The operation of the oscillator is based on the RC time constant of R1 and C1. Let's see how.
Initially, before Vcc is applied, Q1 is OFF. There is no bias voltage on B2 and no TURN ON voltage on E.
Applying Vcc forward biases Q1. The emitter voltage is still 0 V. Q1 is OFF.
Once Vcc is applied, C1 begins to charge, applying a positive voltage on the emitter of Q1.
At this point, the positive voltage is not large enough to turn Q1 ON.
C1 continues to charge until Q1's TURN ON voltage is reached..
When Q1 turns ON, C1 is allowed to discharge through the UJT from B1 to E.
OSCILLATOR FREQUENCY - Frequency equals 1 divided by time. Time equals 1 RC time constant, therefore:
When a sawtooth is measured on the emitter, the oscillator is operating. Now, let's check for normal operation by comparing the calculated and measured frequency of the oscillator.
When Q1 turns ON, C1 is allowed to discharge through the UJT from B1 to E.
C1's voltage drops as it discharges.............................
Once C1's voltage drops below the TURN ON voltage, Q1 turns OFF. C1 no longer discharges.
The cycle repeats. With Q1 OFF, C1 begins to charge............
The voltage on the emitter of Q1 starts at 0 V and increases towards Q1's TURN ON voltage as C1 charges.
Once Q1 turns ON, the emitter voltage drops to 0 V...............
Q1 turns OFF, allowing C1 to charge again......................
The result is a sawtooth waveform on Q1's emitter. The circuit changes +DC power into AC power.
The frequency of the UJT oscillator depends on the charging time of C1, or the RC time constant.
Using 1 TC as the time for one cycle gives an approximation of the frequency of the oscillator.

OSCILLATOR FREQUENCY - The actual frequency of the UJT oscillator depends on the applied voltage, the UJTs eta, and the values of R1 and C1.
ETA - Eta equals the value of: Eta = Rbb1

RESISTOR AND CAPACITOR VALUES - The values of R1 and C1 establish the time required for C1 to change from 0 V to Vcc. The equates to five time constants (5 x R x C). Normally, Q1 will TURN ON at a voltage level less than Vcc.
OSCILLATOR FREQUENCY - Consequently, the time for C1 to charge from 0 V to Q1's TURN ON voltage is less than 5 time constants. Remember, Q1's TURN ON voltage equals eta times Vcc.

OSCILLATOR FREQUENCY - For example, if Vcc is +12 V and Q1's turn on voltage is 8 V, C1 only had to charge from 0 V to 8 V or 67% of the full charge. 67% of full charge is a little more than 1 TC (recall 1 TC equals 63%).
OSCILLATOR FREQUENCY - Normally, using 1 time constant to calculate UJT's oscillator frequency gives results close enough to check for normal operation.

The basic UJT oscillator produces one output signal, a sawtooth wave.
By adding a small resistor to each base circuit, three output signals are produced.
Looking at TP1, the output voltage is a little less than +Vcc as long as Q1 is OFF.
Recall that a UJT acts as a large resistance because the base material is lightly doped. Since R2 is a small value, most of Vcc is dropped across Q1.
When Q1 turns ON, it conducts heavily causing R2 to drop more voltage. This decreases the voltage on B2.
Q1 does not stay ON very long, only the time it takes for C1 to discharge through R3 (which is also very small), the output signal is a pulse.
The negative going pulse has the same frequency of the sawtooth since both rely on the charging and discharging of C1.
The small resistor on B1 also produces a pulse..................
When Q1 is OFF, the voltage on TP2 is approximately 0 V.........
Again, recall that a UJT acts as a large resistance because the base material is lightly doped. R3 being a small value, most of Vcc is dropped across Q1.
When Q1 turns ON, it conducts heavily between E and B1. The voltage drop across R3 becomes larger.
Q1 does not stay ON very long, only the time it takes for C1 to discharge through R3 (which is very small), the output signal is a pulse.
The positive going pulse has the same frequency of the sawtooth since both rely on the charging and discharging of C1.
